blockers.quote: The second fact, about the people who live this: people who remember almost every day of their lives, and Jill Price's own words about it (both to source at G2; planted here, before 60%). You snap at mom over something from years ago; she doesn't remember it at all.
blockers.why: story #6 and story #7: the fact arrives before you act on the misconception, and this use names no expected outcome.
blockers.fix: You repeat Mom's exact words from years ago, expecting recognition and an apology; she genuinely remembers none of it, and the argument worsens. Then Jill Price's sourced words explain why you are still living the old fight, landing directly on your replay within two lines.

suggestions.quote: Your room papered with every page you have read, and the crimson shout from age nine following you into the kitchen, talking over the tea she just brought
suggestions.fix: Make this an active sequence: you leave the papered room expecting the memory to stay there, but the crimson shout follows into the kitchen and covers Mom's present-day tea gesture. Change the shot or action every 2–4 seconds.

suggestions.quote: At eighty, the shout from age nine is as loud as this morning, and so is the morning she taught you to ride a cycle.
suggestions.fix: Clarify that this is a projected consequence: “The room races forward. At eighty, the shout from age nine is still as loud as this morning—and so is the morning she taught you to ride a cycle.”

suggestions.quote:
Do I remember from before the power? Can I still learn new things? Will I go mad?
Does mom remember it too? Is there a cure?
suggestions.fix: Keep the existing answers for backward memory, learning, and Mom. Answer overload when it first occurs without diagnosing it, and add “There is no off switch” to the rule before 0:30 so the cure question is settled where it arises.

keep.quote: Then the question quotes no page; it asks you to apply one to something new, and you freeze.
when someone tells you they forgot, it may be the kindest thing they did
